The university are simply trying to prioritize "diversity." The public usually sees this as a selling point for higher education, but the reality is that in order to maintain visible (ie racial) diversity, the organization is forced to employ a quota system. More highly performing populations (Asians and to a lesser extent Whites) get crowded out, whereas less highly performing populations (Blacks and to a lesser extent Latinos) have less competition to enter and thus lower standards.

Depending on your viewpoint, this is either offensively racist or a benign correction to the social disadvantages that create the performance discrepancy in the first place. My primary criticism is that I think we can get 80% of the benefit from 20% of the effort (and headache): Prioritize entry to those from poorer families, at least for public universities. Private schools are their own clubs and can make their own rules, but public universities should act, at least in part, in the public interest. If education is a means out of poverty, then increasing the priority for the poor applicants would serve the public interest. If an ethnic population is truly disadvantaged, there should be no shortage of poor applicants from said population.

The primary disadvantage of the proposal, as I see it, is that no university would want to implement it. Speaking broadly, poor people typically live in poor neighborhoods with inferior schools, and the local culture typically does little to encourage scholasticism. The perception of a big poverty boost would be that it would reduce the quality of the schools in their academic mission. Plus, majority poor students mean lower tuition and a smaller pool of donors. Also, there is the issue of how much weight to give to socio-economic status and how to determine it.

TIL: The smell during rain after a long, dry period, is called Petrichor.

Since it's raining where I am and hadn't for a long time, the smell was strong and I wanted to know what it was called! Now you all know!

tl;dr

In the article, the authors describe how the smell derives from an oil exuded by certain plants during dry periods, whereupon it is absorbed by clay-based soils and rocks. During rain, the oil is released into the air along with another compound, geosmin, a metabolic by-product of certain Actinobacteria, which is emitted by wet soil, producing the distinctive scent; ozone may also be present if there is lightning.
